title: How do AI Agent workflows (langgraph) know what tools to use?
q_body: Hi I'm currently trying to start to use langgraph and it's really awesome and incredible. I'm slightly confused on a certain subject though, how does langgraph identify tools? How does it know what a tool does? How can I convey the purpose of the tool in order to be clearer? From what I understand, its only means is to read the function and the input it gets. Does this mean I should be making super long function names in order to explain the finer details? This might be a very simple solution but I'm confused as to how it's able to fetch further information on the tool provided. From the tutorial they use the following example: @tool def human_assistance(query: str) -> str: """Request assistance from a human.""" human_response = interrupt({"query": query}) return human_response["data"] I don't see how it's able to understand from the function name that human_assitance is capable to interrupt a query and tell the ai graph that it will get a response from a human. For all I know, it could interpret it as "human_assistance" -> "human helps me" -> "human does the work" and not that it will have to continue querying. This is a bit of a far fetch but it's to better understand more complex tools and how to properly convey to an LLM its function.

title: Which Python GUI frameworks expose native Windows UI Automation properties correctly?
q_body: I am developing a Windows desktop GUI application in Python and need proper compatibility with screen readers such as NVDA and JAWS. title: Getting mypy to recognize tuple of certain length
q_body: Mypy triggers the following error: Incompatible return value type (got "tuple[int | None, ...]", expected "tuple[int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None]") [return-value] I presume this is because mypy doesn't recognize the number of elements in the list before converting to tuple. Is there a way to get mypy see this tuple properly (not just adding an ignore)? T_day = int | None T_week = tuple[T_day, T_day, T_day, T_day, T_day, T_day, T_day] def shift_week(dayofweek: int, week: T_week) -> T_week: week_shifted: list[T_day] = [] week_shifted.extend(week[dayofweek:]) week_shifted.extend(week[:dayofweek]) return tuple(week_shifted) # <- mypy error # Incompatible return value type (got "tuple[int | None, ...]", expected "tuple[int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None, int | None]") [return-value] week = (1,2,3,4,5,6,7) rt = shift_week(3, week) print(rt) (4, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3) Key point: the annotation of T_week needs to contain 7 T_day . I considered simply using tuple[T_day, ...] but doing so would cause mypy to lose the ability to spot when someone has built a tuple of the wrong size. I had hoped adding assert len(week_shifted) == 7 would work, but mypy isn't that clever.

title: Is it possible to pass in the base object when calling a sub function?
q_body: I had a bug with the following code and figured out the reason: myset = set(["A", "C", "B"]) # Original Code: Fails output: None print(list(myset).sort()) list.sort() is an in-place sort with no return value, and this is passing the return from the sort() call to print; which is why this code doesn't work. To fix it, I can obviously use the sorted function or write my own: # Method 1: Works out: ['A', 'B', 'C'] print(sorted(myset)) # Method 2: Works out: ['A', 'B', 'C'] def mysetsort(s): l = list(s) l.sort() return l print(mysetsort(s)) Is there any way to do this along the lines of the original buggy inline implementation, i.e. use sort() on the temporary list from the cast, but pass in/return the temporary (sorted) object?

Are these supposed to be identical?

title: Why is the greyscale & B&W images created by Pillow giving a numpy.ndarray that has a 3D shape?
q_body: Input: import numpy as np from PIL import Image with Image.open("testimage.png") as img: img.convert('L') # convert to greyscale #img.convert('1') # convert to B&W image_pil = np.asarray(img) print(f'{image_pil.shape=}') Output: image_pil.shape=(266, 485, 3) Question: Why is the shape of image_pil not (266, 485) or (266, 485, 1) ? I was expecting a 2D greyscale image but it gave a shape of (266, 485, 3) indicate that it is still a RGB image. Also, .convert('1') had the same outcome. Why are they not shaped (266, 485) ?

title: What exercises improve problem-solving skills in programming?
q_body: I am currently learning programming and want to improve my problem-solving ability rather than just memorizing syntax or copying solutions. I understand that strong programming skills come from being able to analyze problems, break them into smaller parts, and design logical solutions. However, I’m not sure what kinds of exercises are most effective for developing this skill. For example, some people recommend solving algorithm problems, while others suggest building small projects or practicing debugging.
